<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hkn_is_Mobius_sum_of_Franel_integrals} $\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right)$ is a k-fold Möbius sum of Franel integrals of order $k$.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:expr1_Hkn}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right):=(-1)^k\sum_{d_1\mid n}\mu(d_1)\cdots\sum_{d_k\mid n}\mu(d_k) \mathcal{F}\left( \frac{n}{d_1},\ldots,\frac{n}{d_k} \right),
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
With $B(x)={x}-1/2$ the first periodic Bernoulli polynomial, we have $\nu_n(x)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)B(x)$ since $\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)=0$ (see \cite{hardy1979introduction}, Theorem 263). Therefore,
\[
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right):=(-1)^k\sum_{d_1\mid n}\mu(d_1)\cdots\sum_{d_k\mid n}\mu(d_k) \int_0^1\prod_{i=1}^kB\left(\frac{n}{d_i} t\right)dt ,
\]
but
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Franel_with_B_or_dp}
\int_0^1\prod_{i=1}^kB\left(\frac{n}{d_i} t\right)dt=\int_0^1\prod_{i=1}^k\left(\!\!\left(\frac{n}{d_i} t\right)\!\!\right)dt,
\end{equation}
since the integrands are equal appart from a finite number of points.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hkn0_kodd} If $k$ is odd, $\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right)=0$ for any positive integer $n$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
A direct consequence of Franel integrals being equal to zero with an odd number of parameters in Equation (\ref{eq:expr1_Hkn}). In Equation (\ref{eq:Franel_sum_lattice_points}) when $a_1b_1+\cdots + a_kb_k=0$, we also have $a_1(-b_1)+\cdots + a_k(-b_k)=0$, and the two points lead to the contribution $\frac{1}{b_1\cdots b_k}+(-1)^k\frac{1}{b_1\cdots b_k}$ which is zero for odd $k$. Therefore all points contributions can be grouped by pairs that contribute to 0 in the sum.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hkn_egal_Hkradn} For any positive integers $k$ and $n$
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right)=\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)\right).
\label{eq:Hkn_egal_Hkradn}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The Mobius function is zero on integers with a square factor, hence
\[
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right):=(-1)^k\sum_{d_1\mid \textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}\mu(d_1)\cdots\sum_{d_k\mid \textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}\mu(d_k) \mathcal{F}\left( \frac{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}{d_1}\frac{n}{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)},\ldots,\frac{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}{d_k}\frac{n}{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)} \right),
\]
but $\mathcal{F}\left( \frac{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}{d_1}\frac{n}{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)},\ldots,\frac{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}{d_k}\frac{n}{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)} \right)=\mathcal{F}\left( \frac{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}{d_1},\ldots,\frac{\textbf{rad}\left( n \right)}{d_k} \right)$ as a general property of Franel integrals which is easily seen from Equation (\ref{eq:Franel_sum_lattice_points}): when $a_1b_1+\cdots + a_kb_k=0$ we also have $ca_1b_1+\cdots + ca_kb_k=0$ for any integer $c$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
For any odd integer $m$,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(2m\right)=\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(m\right).
\label{eq:Hk2m_egal_Hkm}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From Equation (\ref{eq:Hkn}), $\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(2m\right)=\int_0^1\left(-\nu_{2m}(2mt)\right)^kdt$. Since $\mu(2d)=-\mu(d)$, we see that
\[ \nu_{2m}(2mt) = \sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)\left(B\left(2\frac{m}{d}t\right)-B\left(\frac{m}{d}t\right)\right).\]
We use lemma 1, page 78, in \cite{delange1968distribution}, with $n=2$, to see that $B(2x)-B(x)=B\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)$. Also, because $\frac{m}{d}$ is odd, whe have $B\left(\frac{m}{d}t+\frac{1}{2}\right)=B\left(\frac{m}{d}\left(t+\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)$. Thus $\nu_{2m}(2mt)=\nu_{m}\left(m\left(t+\frac{1}{2}\right)\right)$. The change of variable $u=t+\frac{1}{2}$, leads to $\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(2m\right)=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left(-\nu_{m}(mu)\right)^kdu$, which ends the proof, since $u\mapsto \nu_{m}(mu)$ has period 1.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:nuna_plus_nunma} Let $n$ be an integer greater than or equal to 2 and $a\in t\left( n \right)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nuna_plus_nunma}
\nu_n(a)+\nu_n(-a)=-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
let $d\mid n$. If $d=1$ then $\left\{ \frac{a}{d} \right\}+\left\{ \frac{-a}{d} \right\}=0$. If $d>1$, $\frac{a}{d}$ is not an integer and therefore $\left\{ \frac{a}{d} \right\}+\left\{ \frac{-a}{d} \right\}=1$. It follows that
\begin{equation*}
\nu_n(a)+\nu_n(-a) = \sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d>1}}\mu(d) = \left(\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\right) - \mu(1) = -1.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:nunknpa} Let $n\geq 2$ be an integer, $k$ an integer and $a\in t\left( n \right)$, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nunknpa}
\nu_n(kn+a)=\nu_n(a).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
It comes from a direct calculation and the fact that $k\frac{n}{d}$ is an integer when $d\mid n$:
\begin{equation*}
\nu_n(kn+a) =\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\left\{ k\frac{n}{d}+\frac{a}{d} \right\} = \nu_n(a).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:Hkn_fn_Vkp1n} Let $k$ and $n$ be positive integers,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right) = - \frac{1+(-1)^k}{(k+1)\phi(n)} V_{k+1}(n).
\label{eq:Hkn_fn_Vkp1n}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The function $t\mapsto \left(\theta_n(nt)-\phi(n)t\right)^k$ is periodic of period 1, therefore for any real number $x$,
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right)=\int_{x}^{x+1}\left(\theta_n(nt)-\phi(n)t\right)^kdt.
\end{equation*}
In particular, for $x=\frac{-1}{n}$, with the convention that $u_0=-1$,
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{\phi(n)-1}\int_{\frac{u_i}{n}}^{\frac{u_{i+1}}{n}}\left(i-\phi(n)t\right)^kdt \\
&=\frac{-1}{(k+1)\phi(n)}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\phi(n)-1} \left(i-\frac{\phi(n)}{n}u_{i+1}\right)^{k+1} - \sum_{i=0}^{\phi(n)-1} \left(i-\frac{\phi(n)}{n}u_{i}\right)^{k+1} \right).
\end{align*}
We shall look separately at the two sums, say respectively, $A$ and $B$. Regarding the first sum
\begin{align*}
A
&= \sum_{i=1}^{\phi(n)} \left(i-\frac{\phi(n)}{n}u_i-1\right)^{k+1}         &\text{change of index}\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \left(\theta_n(a)-\frac{\phi(n)}{n}a-1\right)^{k+1} &\text{summing over }t\left( n \right)\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \left(-\nu_n(a)-1\right)^{k+1}                      &\text{from Equation (\ref{eq:formula_thetanx_plus_nunx})}\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \nu_n(-a)^{k+1}                                     &\text{from Equation (\ref{eq:nuna_plus_nunma})}\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \nu_n(n-a)^{k+1}                                    &\text{from Equation (\ref{eq:nunknpa})}\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \nu_n(a)^{k+1}.                                     &\text{reverse order sum}
\end{align*}
Regarding the second sum, let's first remark that we have
\begin{equation*}
i+\phi(n)-\frac{\phi(n)}{n}u_{i+\phi(n)} = i-\frac{\phi(n)}{n}u_i,
\end{equation*}
hence the sum is constant provided it spans over $\phi(n)$ consecutive indexes.
\begin{align*}
B
&= \sum_{i=1}^{\phi(n)} \left(i-u_{i}\frac{\phi(n)}{n}\right)^{k+1}       &\text{from the remark above}\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \left(\theta_n(a)-a\frac{\phi(n)}{n}\right)^{k+1} &\text{summing over }t\left( n \right)\\
&= \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \left(-\nu_n(a)\right)^{k+1}                      &\text{from Equation (\ref{eq:formula_thetanx_plus_nunx})}\\
&= (-1)^{k+1} \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \nu_n(a)^{k+1}.                             &
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The formula implies that $\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(n\right)$ vanishes when $k$ is odd, consistently with Proposition \ref{prop:Hkn0_kodd}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Let $p$ be a prime number and $k$ and $\alpha$ two positive integers, we have the following identity:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(p^\alpha\right) = \frac{1+(-1)^k}{(k+1)(k+2)(p-1)}\sum_{j=0}^{k+1}\binom{k+2}{j}B_j p^{1-j}.
\label{eq:Hkp_alpha}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
From Proposition \ref{prop:Hkn_egal_Hkradn}, there is $\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(p^\alpha\right)=\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(p\right)$. Given that $p$ is a prime number, we have $\nu_p(i)=-\frac{i}{p}$ from Equation (\ref{eq:nu_n}). In that case, Equation (\ref{eq:Hkn_fn_Vkp1n}) simplifies to
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{H}_{k}\left(p\right) = - \frac{1+(-1)^k}{(k+1)(p-1)} \left(\frac{-1}{p} \right)^{k+1} \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} i^k.
                       
\end{equation*}
We get Equation (\ref{eq:Hkp_alpha}) after using Faulhaber's formula for sums of powers of consecutive integers that can be found in Equation 6.78 page 283 in \cite{graham1989donald}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
For any integer $n\geq 2$ and for any positive integer $k$
\begin{equation}
\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} \left( {\nu_n(a)}^k + (-1)^{k+1}\left(1+\nu_n(a)\right)^k \right) = 0.
\label{eq:relation_liante_Vk}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Given that $a\mapsto n-a$ is a bijection of $t\left( n \right)$, we have
\[
\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} {\nu_n(a)}^k=\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} {\nu_n(n-a)}^k,
\]
and then we use Propositions \ref{prop:nunknpa} and \ref{prop:nuna_plus_nunma}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
An even $k=2a$ for some integer $a$ happens to provide the same equation as $k=2a-1$ which is easily seen from Equation (\ref{eq:relation_liante_Vk}).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
From Theorem \ref{thm:Hkn_fn_Vkp1n}, we see that $\mathcal{H}_{4}\left(n\right)$ depends on $V_5(n)$. From Equation (\ref{eq:rel_V5n_V4n_etc}), we see that $V_5(n)$ depends on $V_i(n)$ for $0\leq i\leq 4$. The Equations (\ref{eq:formula_V0n}), (\ref{eq:formula_V1n}), (\ref{eq:formula_V2n}) and (\ref{eq:formula_V3n}) lead to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relation_V5n_V4n}
V_5(n) = -\frac{5}{2}V_4(n)+\frac{\phi(n)}{12}\left( 5\cdot2^{\omega(n)-1}\frac{\phi(n)}{n}-1\right).
\end{equation}
This means that having a formula for either $V_4(n)$ or $V_5(n)$ would allow for the calculation $\mathcal{H}_{4}\left(n\right)$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The sum for $a\in t\left( n \right)$ of the square of Equation (\ref{eq:formula_thetanx_plus_nunx}) evaluated at $x=a$ provides
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)}\theta_n(a)^2+\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)}\nu_n(a)^2+2\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)}\theta_n(a)\nu_n(a) = \frac{\phi(n)^2}{n^2} \sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} a^2.
\end{equation*}
All the sums but one are known\footnote{The first sum is just $\sum_{j=1}^{\phi(n)}j^2$; the second is Equation (\ref{eq:formula_V2n}); the last one, $\sum_{a\in t\left( n \right)} a^2$ can be found in \cite{apostol1976introduction}.} and therefore we get a formula for the unknown sum
\begin{equation}\label{eq:formula_sum_thetananuna}
\sum_{a \in t\left( n \right)}\theta_n(a)\nu_n(a)=\frac{{(-1)}^{\omega(n)}}{12n}\phi(n)^3-\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2^{\omega(n)}}{24n}\right)\phi(n)^2-\frac{1}{6}\phi(n).
\end{equation}
Now, observe that
\begin{equation*}
\theta_n(a)a = \theta_n(a) \frac{n}{\phi(n)}\left(\theta_n(a)+\nu_n(a)\right),
\end{equation*}
and therefore, summing over $a\in t\left( n \right)$
\[
\sum_{a \in t\left( n \right)}\theta_n(a)a=\frac{n}{\phi(n)}\left(\sum_{a \in t\left( n \right)}{\theta_n(a)}^2+\sum_{a \in t\left( n \right)}\theta_n(a)\nu_n(a)\right),
\]
which allows for a calculation of Spence formula since the two sums on the right-hand side are known.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:formula_X_N_a_b} Let $a$, $b$ and $N$ be positive integers such that $a\mid N$ and $b\mid N$, we have the following formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:X_N_a_b}
X_N(\{a,b\})=\frac{N}{4}(a-1)(b-1)+\frac{N}{12}\left(\mathrm{gcd}\left( a,b \right)^2-1\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $g=\mathrm{gcd}\left( a,b \right)$. We can write that $a=gu$ and $b=gv$ for some integers $u$ and $v$. Since $a\mid N$ and $g\mid a$, $g\mid N$ and there exists an integer $M$ such that $N=gM$. Now,
\begin{align*}
X_N(\{a,b\}) &= \sum_{q=0}^{M-1}\sum_{s=0}^{g-1} ((gq+s)\bmod gu)((gq+s)\bmod gv) \\
&= \sum_{q=0}^{M-1}\sum_{s=0}^{g-1} (g(q\bmod u)+s)(g(q\bmod v)+s).
\end{align*}
Note that, $a\mid N$ means that there exists an integer $\theta$ such that $N=a\theta=gu\theta$, but $N=gM$ thus $u\mid M$. Similarly $v\mid M$, but $\mathrm{gcd}\left( u,v \right)=1$ means that $uv\mid M$. Since $M$ is a multiple of $uv$ the sums over $q$ can easily be evaluated as repeated elementary sums and the result follows.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
We see that the formula vanishes for $a=1$ or $b=1$, as expected. We also see that $a=b=N$ leads to the formula of a sum of squares, as expected.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:formula_X_N_a_b_c} Let $a$, $b$, $c$ and $N$ be positive integers such that $a\mid N$, $b\mid N$ and $c\mid N$, we have the following formula
\begin{multline}\label{eq:W_N_a_b_c}
X_N(\{a,b,c\})=\frac{N}{8}(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)+\frac{N}{24}(a-1)\left(\mathrm{gcd}\left( b,c \right)^2-1\right)+\\
\frac{N}{24}(b-1)\left(\mathrm{gcd}\left( a,c \right)^2-1\right)+\frac{N}{24}(c-1)\left(\mathrm{gcd}\left( a,b \right)^2-1\right).
\end{multline}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We write the sum in the reverse order, observing that $(n-r)\bmod a=a-1-r\bmod a$. The result follows easily after development of the product under the sum. The same sum appears with a negative sign on the right-hand side. We then use the previous formulas for one and two modulos.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
We see that the formula vanishes for $a=1$ or $b=1$, as expected. We also see that $a=b=N$ leads to the formula of a sum of cubes, as expected.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
If $N$ is an integer and if $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are divisors of $N$, then $X_N(a,b,c,d)$ does not have a polynomial closed form formula in $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and in any greatest common divisors of any combination of these variables, pairs, triplets or quadruplets.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:Franel4_as_function_of_W4}
Let $E=\left\{a,b,c,d\right\}$ be a multiset of 4 positive integers, and $N$ be any common multiple of $a,b,c,d$. For any unordered pair $\{x,y\}\subset E$, we write $\{z,t\}$ the unordered pair $E\setminus \{x,y\}$.
\begin{multline}\label{eq:Franel_ordre_4}
\mathcal{F}\left( a,b,c,d \right)=\frac{W_N(E)}{N^5}+\frac{abcd}{30N^4} -\frac{1}{72N^2}\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset E} \frac{{\mathrm{gcd}\left( x,y \right)}^2}{xy}zt + \\
\frac{1}{48N}\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset E} \frac{{\mathrm{gcd}\left( x,y \right)}^2}{xy}(z+t-M) -\frac{1}{24N^2}\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset E}xy +\frac{1}{16N}\sum_{x\in E}x-\frac{1}{16}.
\end{multline}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:Somme_Mobius_W_4_m}
Let $m\ge2$ be a square-free integer; we define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Somme_Mobius_W_4_m}
\mathcal{W}_4(m) := \frac{1}{m^5} \sum_{d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4\mid m} \mu(d_1) \mu(d_2) \mu(d_3) \mu(d_4) W_m\left( \frac m{d_1},\frac m{d_2},\frac m{d_3},\frac m{d_4} \right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:expression_H_4_m}
Let $m\ge2$ be a square-free integer. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:expression_H_4_m}
\mathcal{H}_{4}\left(m\right) = \mathcal{W}_4(m) + \frac{1}{60m}\left(\frac{\phi(m)}{m}\right)^3\left(2\phi(m)-5m2^{\omega(m)}\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
If we consider Equation (\ref{eq:expr1_Hkn}), with $k=4$, we see that the same value $m$ can be used\footnote{Consistently with the comment made in section \ref{sec:Franel_and_Dedekind}.}, as a multiple of the least common multiple of the integers $\frac{n}{d_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq 4$. Now, looking at the right-hand side of Equation (\ref{eq:Franel_ordre_4}), it is clear that any term that does not depend simultaneously on $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_3$ and $d_4$ will have a zero fourfold Möbius sum, since we can factor at least one sum of the type $\sum_{d\mid m}\mu(d)$ which is equal to zero (See Theorem 263 in \cite{hardy1979introduction}). We immediately have
\[
\sum_{d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4\mid m} \mu(d_1) \mu(d_2) \mu(d_3) \mu(d_4) \frac{1}{30d_1d_2d_3d_4} = \frac{1}{30}\left(\frac{\phi(m)}{m}\right)^4.
\]
Also, the summand of the sum
\[
\sum_{d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4\mid m} \mu(d_1) \mu(d_2) \mu(d_3) \mu(d_4) {\mathrm{gcd}\left( \frac{m}{d_1},\frac{m}{d_2} \right)}^2\frac{d_1d_2}{d_3d_4},
\]
is a multiplicative function, and there is no difficulty in proving that is equal to
\[
2^{\omega(m)}\frac{\phi(m)^3}{m}.
\]
There are 6 terms of that form, since there are 6 choices of unordered pairs in a set of 4 elements; their total contribution is 
\[
-\frac{1}{72m^2}\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset E} \frac{{\mathrm{gcd}\left( x,y \right)}^2}{xy}zt = -\frac{2^{\omega(m)}}{12}\left(\frac{\phi(m)}{m}\right)^3.
\]
which proves Equation (\ref{eq:expression_H_4_m}).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Let $p$ be a prime number, the Equation (\ref{eq:expression_H_4_m}) with $m=p$ gives
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{r=0}^{p-1}r^4 - \frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{p-1}{p}\right)^3 + \frac{1}{30}\left(\frac{p-1}{p}\right)^4,
\end{equation*}
which simplifies to 
\[
\frac{p-1}{30}\left(\frac{2}{p}-\frac{2}{p^2}-\frac{1}{p^3}\right),
\]
which is consistent with Equation (\ref{eq:H4p_p_prime}).
<!-- end remark-6 -->
